title: Halley's Comet Leaves a Trail of Shooting Stars
summary:
You do not need to wait for Halley's Comet to visit to see its fireworks. This week, Earth passed through a trail of dusty debris left behind by the famous comet, and the crumbs put on a show as the Orionid meteor shower reached its peak.

On Oct. 21, astrophotographer Tim McCollum captured a spectacular composite image above Toccoa, Georgia. Between 3 and 4 a.m., he photographed three vivid Orionid meteors streaking across the sky. Each shooting star appears to race away from the shower's radiant — the point in the sky the meteors seem to come from — which sits near Betelgeuse, the red giant star in the constellation Orion. Halley's Comet itself is more than 3 billion miles from Earth right now, but the particles it shed still carve bright paths through the autumn sky when they hit our atmosphere.

McCollum's picture holds more wonders. Orion's Belt glistens beside the glow of the Orion Nebula, one of the closest major star-forming regions to Earth. The Rosette Nebula also appears, nestled in the dense starfields and dust lanes of the Milky Way, which slants diagonally across the image. Catching a shooting star on camera takes skill, luck and patience. McCollum used a star tracker to keep his camera fixed on the radiant and took many 30-second exposures, later combining them into one image with astrophoto software.

If you missed the peak, there is still time: the Orionid shower stays active until Nov. 7. Head outside on a clear night and you might spot one of Halley's dazzling leftovers — or even a 'Halloween Fireball' from the Taurid meteor shower, made from debris of Comet 2P/Encke.
why_it_matters: Meteor showers let anyone watch space debris burn up in our atmosphere with no equipment at all, connecting everyday skywatchers to a famous comet that is now billions of miles away. They also give photographers a predictable chance to capture the crumbs comets leave behind.

background_read: A meteor shower happens when Earth passes through a trail of dusty debris left behind by a comet, and the tiny particles burn bright as they hit the atmosphere.
Halley's Comet sheds such crumbs as it travels, so its leftovers can light up the sky even when the comet itself is billions of miles away.
The Orionid shower is named for Orion, because its meteors seem to race away from a point called the radiant near that constellation.
Photographers catch the brief streaks by keeping a camera fixed on the radiant and combining many long exposures into a single composite image.
Article_Structure: LEAD: Earth passed through dusty debris left by Halley's Comet, putting on the Orionid meteor shower at its peak
KEY EVENT: Astrophotographer Tim McCollum captured three vivid Orionid meteors above Toccoa, Georgia, on Oct. 21
├─ WHERE: Above Toccoa, Georgia, with the radiant near Betelgeuse in the constellation Orion
└─ HOW: A star tracker held the camera on the radiant while many 30-second exposures were combined into one composite image
EVIDENCE: The composite also shows Orion's Belt, the Orion Nebula, the Rosette Nebula and the Milky Way's dense starfields
OPEN QUESTION: Whether clear skies will let viewers catch more meteors — or a Taurid 'Halloween Fireball' — before the shower ends after Nov. 7
